p: Jordan passed her medical exam with no limits.
Marisol put her to work on an oil change with Biscuit's engine open, and quizzed her on carburetor ice, spark plugs and the electrical system.
Reading every line of the maintenance logbooks, Jordan found an emergency beacon battery whose replacement date had passed in March, after Danny died. Marisol replaced it before anyone flew.
On a damp May morning the engine iced up on a long descent and Jordan cleared it with carb heat. Danny's notebook had the same scare, in the same airplane.
Then Marisol showed her a lumpy twist of safety wire from a year of Saturdays Danny spent in her hangar after her divorce, and nobody in the family had known.
Abby Strand. Jordan's instructor. Blunt, quick, and hard to impress.
Walt Herrera. The club's safety officer, and the partner Jordan most needs to win over.
Russ Kim. The fourth partner, who flew Biscuit over the mountains in April.
Marisol Tran. The club's mechanic, who's started letting Jordan in.
Ellie Reyes. Danny and Claire's daughter. She's nine.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow, Ellie's mother.

Wednesday night Jordan sat at her kitchen table in Aurora with a mug of tea going cold and the Centennial forecast open on her laptop, and for the first ten minutes it looked like a ransom note. Abby had booked her for Thursday at seven, if the weather played nice, on one condition: check the TAF before you text me.

The Centennial forecast, three lines of letters and numbers. The first line starts TAF, KAPA, one three two three two zero Zulu, one four zero zero slash one four two four, then the wind and clouds: three three zero at eight knots, more than six miles, a few clouds at ten thousand. The second line, from oh nine hundred Zulu, has light and variable wind and a clear sky, and the third starts F M one four one five zero zero.

She did what she always did with a call she didn't understand. She took it apart. The FAA's Aviation Weather Handbook was a free PDF, a few hundred pages longer than any protocol binder she'd ever been handed, and she read the section on terminal forecasts twice, the second time with a pen.

TAF, then the airport. Then one three two three two zero Zulu: the forecast was finished on the 13th at 2320 Zulu, which the handbook said was UTC, which a different website said was six hours ahead of Colorado in the summer. Then fourteen hundred slash fourteen twenty four, good from midnight Zulu on the 14th to midnight Zulu at the end of it. They wrote midnight at the end as 24 so nobody would confuse it with the start. She liked that. It was the kind of rule a tired person had written for other tired people.

F M one four one five zero zero meant from 1500 Zulu on the 14th. Nine in the morning, her time. Northwest at ten knots, more than six miles visibility, a few clouds at eight thousand feet. Her lesson was at seven. She'd be back on the ground by eight thirty, before any of it.
She texted Abby a screenshot with her decode typed underneath, line by line, the way she'd hand off a patient. The reply came at 10:06.
A text from Abby Strand. Not bad. Check it again when you wake up. A TAF is a forecast. The weather didn't read it.

Danny's green notebook sat at the other end of the table under her keys. She'd been reading it a few entries at a time, in order, and she'd only skipped ahead once. She set her alarm for 5:55 and went to bed.
Abby's Ground School: reading the sky and the paperwork about it.
Rising air cools: lapse rates, cloud bases, and stability.

You canceled. I'm still a little stunned. You're here and the coffee's on, so this is weather school, and it starts with one idea that runs underneath everything else I'm going to tell you today. Air that rises cools off. Air that sinks warms up. Keep that in your pocket.

Start with the standard atmosphere, which is the average day nobody ever actually gets. At sea level it's 15°C and 29.92 inches of mercury, and the temperature drops about 2°C for every 1,000 feet you climb, which is 3.5°F. How fast the temperature drops with height is called the lapse rate. Sometimes it doesn't drop at all. A layer where it gets warmer as you go up is an inversion, and you'll meet them on clear, calm mornings out here, a lid of warm air sitting on top of cold air on the ground.

Now push a bubble of air upward. As long as it isn't saturated it cools about 3°C per 1,000 feet. That's the dry adiabatic rate. Its dewpoint drops too, but slowly, only about half a degree per 1,000. So the temperature and the dewpoint close in on each other by roughly 2.5°C every 1,000 feet. When they meet, the water vapor condenses and you get a cloud. That's where the cloud base estimate comes from. Take the surface temperature minus the dewpoint in Celsius, divide by 2.5, multiply by 1,000, and you've got the base in feet above the ground. The PHAK does it in Fahrenheit: spread divided by 4.4, times 1,000. Same answer, different units. This morning it was 12 and minus 3, a spread of 15. Fifteen divided by 2.5 is 6, so about 6,000 feet AGL. Add our field elevation, 5,885, and that's about 11,900 MSL. People blow that question on the test by forgetting the estimate comes out AGL. It works best for puffy cumulus built by heating from the ground. It's an estimate, so don't go setting your altimeter by it.

Once the bubble's saturated it keeps cooling, but slower, because condensation gives off heat. That's the moist adiabatic rate. It runs anywhere from about 1.2 to 3°C per 1,000 depending on temperature, and the handbook uses 2 for its examples.

Stability is just this question: if you shove some air up, does it want to come back down, or does it keep going? If it ends up colder than the air around it, it sinks back. That's stable. If it ends up warmer, it keeps rising on its own. Unstable. A steeper lapse rate means less stable air. Stable air gives you flat layers of stratus, a smooth ride, steady rain or drizzle, and poor visibility, because the haze and smoke can't rise out of it. Unstable air gives you cumulus, showers, bumps, and good visibility outside the showers. Sun heating the ground makes the low air less stable. Night cooling makes it more stable. That's why your 7 a.m. lessons are smooth and the plains at 2 p.m. feel like the inside of a dryer.

How the exam asks it. Know the cloud base formula in both units, and that the answer is AGL. Know the stable versus unstable lists cold. An inversion means stable air near the ground, often with poor visibility under it.

An air mass is a giant blob of air that parked somewhere long enough to pick up the local personality. Canada makes them cold and dry. The Gulf makes them warm and sticky. Two of them bump, and the seam between them is a front, and that seam is where most of your weather lives.

Cold front first. Heavy cold air bulldozes in underneath the warm air and shoves it up, hard. The edge is steep, and the thing moves, 25 to 30 miles an hour on a typical day. If the warm air it's lifting is unstable you get a skinny line of showers and storms right on the edge. Once it's through, it gets colder, the barometer climbs, the wind turns gusty and the sky goes blue and clean. Warm fronts are the slow ones, 10 to 25 miles an hour, warm air riding up a long gentle ramp of cold air. Their weather shows up way early, hundreds of miles out sometimes. Layers of gray. Drizzle that won't quit. Fog, lousy visibility. In summer there can be thunderstorms buried in those layers where you can't see them. Stationary fronts sit. An occluded front is what you call it when a cold front runs down a warm one and catches it.

Here's the one fact to keep: whatever the front, the wind shifts when it passes. Temperature usually changes. Pressure drops on the way in and comes back up after. The test will ask what you can always count on, and the answer is the wind shift.

Our cold fronts mostly don't come over the mountains. They sneak down the plains from the north or northeast, and the wind behind them turns east. On the Front Range, east is uphill. That wind shoves damp air up the slope, the air cools as it climbs, and the whole city ends up under low cloud and fog for a day. Remember that, we'll need it. West wind's the reverse. Downhill, so it warms and dries out as it sinks, which is exactly why it was 12 degrees and a dewpoint of minus 3 out there at six this morning.
How the exam asks it. Cold front: fast, steep, showery, clearing behind. Warm front: slow, gentle, layered, low visibility ahead. Every front: a wind shift.
The METAR, one group at a time.
This is the one from this morning. I wrote it across the whole whiteboard, so read along with me:
METAR KAPA 141153Z 31016G27KT 10SM FEW080 SCT120 12/M03 A3002 RMK AO2 PK WND 31031/1128 SLP148 T01171028

KAPA is us. 141153Z is the 14th of the month at 1153 Zulu, which was 5:53 this morning. If you see AUTO after the time, nobody human was involved. COR means it's a correction. The routine report comes out once an hour. A SPECI is a special one, sent between hours when something changes enough to matter.

31016G27KT: wind from 310 degrees true, 16 knots, gusting 27. True, not magnetic. The METAR and the TAF give you wind direction from true north. The ATIS and the tower give it to you magnetic, because that's what your runways and your compass use. Here the difference is about 8 degrees, which usually doesn't matter much and occasionally decides a crosswind question on the test. VRB means variable. 00000KT means calm.

10SM is visibility in statute miles. Weather goes next when there is any. A minus sign is light, a plus sign is heavy, VC means in the vicinity, and then the codes: RA rain, SN snow, BR mist, FG fog, HZ haze, FU smoke, TS thunderstorm, SH showers, FZ freezing. They stack, so +TSRA is a thunderstorm with heavy rain.

Clouds: FEW is one or two eighths of the sky, SCT is three or four, BKN is five to seven, OVC is all of it. The number is the height of the base in hundreds of feet above the ground. FEW080 is a few clouds at 8,000 AGL. The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, or a vertical visibility if the sky's obscured, VV002 for example. FEW and SCT don't count. So this morning had no ceiling at all. If you see CB or TCU stuck on a layer, that's cumulonimbus or towering cumulus, and I want you to notice it every time.

12/M03 is temperature and dewpoint in Celsius. M means minus. A3002 is the altimeter setting, 30.02. Then RMK, remarks, which is the part everybody skips and shouldn't. AO2 means an automated station with a precipitation discriminator, a sensor that can tell rain from snow. AO1 can't. PK WND 31031/1128 is a peak wind from 310 at 31 knots at 28 minutes after 11 Zulu. SLP148 is sea level pressure in millibars with the front digits chopped off. Put the 10 back on (or a 9 if the number is 500 or more) and it's 1014.8. And T01171028 is the temperature and dewpoint to a tenth of a degree. The 0 means positive, so 11.7. The 1 means negative, so the dewpoint is minus 2.8. Those tenths are what you want for the cloud base math.
How the exam asks it. Expect a full METAR to decode. Watch for true wind, heights in hundreds of feet AGL, the ceiling being the lowest BKN or OVC, and the M prefix for negative temperatures.
The TAF, and what time it really is.

A TAF is a forecast for the airport, specifically the area within 5 statute miles of the middle of its runways. Not the practice area. Not the mountains. Routine ones come out four times a day, built around 00, 06, 12, and 18 Zulu, and each one's issued 20 to 40 minutes before it starts. Most run 24 hours. Big airports like Denver International get 30.
TAF KAPA 141120Z 1412/1512 31016G27KT P6SM FEW080 SCT120 FM141600 32020G32KT P6SM SCT100 FM150200 33010KT P6SM SKC

141120Z is when it was finished. 1412/1512 is the valid period: the 14th at 12 Zulu until the 15th at 12 Zulu. Then the first forecast line uses the same codes as a METAR, with one new one. P6SM means more than 6 miles.

FM141600 means from the 14th at 1600 Zulu, and everything after it is brand new. An FM line is self contained. The whole forecast before it is thrown out and replaced, even the parts that didn't change. TEMPO is different. TEMPO means temporary changes that are more likely than not, that each last one hour or less, and that together cover less than half of the time it lists. A TEMPO line only lists the things that change. PROB30 means a 30 percent chance, and the NWS only uses it for thunderstorms or precipitation. It's the only probability group you'll see in an American TAF. If an amended forecast comes out, it says TAF AMD and it replaces the old one right then. And sometimes there's a WS group at the end of a line. That's low level wind shear, forecast, not observed.

Now the part that bites people. Every time in these products is Zulu. In the summer, Colorado's on Mountain Daylight Time, which is six hours behind Zulu. In the winter, Mountain Standard, seven hours. So to get to local, you subtract. FM141600 is ten in the morning today. Not four in the afternoon. Last night's forecast had the wind coming at 1500 Zulu, nine o'clock. This morning's had it already here, 16 gusting 27, from the very first line. Same airport, same day, two forecasts twelve hours apart. Read the newest one.

How the exam asks it. Decode valid periods and change groups. FM replaces everything. TEMPO is short and temporary. PROB30 is a 30 percent chance. And convert Zulu correctly before you decide anything.
Winds aloft and the prog charts.

The winds and temperatures aloft forecast is called the FB. It's computer made, comes out four times a day, and gives one number for each of three time blocks. The handbook itself calls it old fashioned next to what your flight planning app pulls in from the models, and it's right, but the test loves it, so here we go.

Each group is direction in tens of degrees true, then speed in knots, then temperature in Celsius. 2614+05 is 260 degrees at 14 knots, plus 5. If you see 9900, that's light and variable, under 5 knots. If the speed is 100 knots or more, they add 50 to the direction and knock 100 off the speed so it still fits in four digits. So 7545 is 250 degrees at 145 knots. Your tell is a direction that looks impossible, anything past 36. Subtract 50 from it and add 100 to the speed. 7799 means 199 knots or more. Above 24,000 feet the minus sign gets dropped, because it's always below zero up there.

See the blanks? Denver International sits at 5,434 feet. They don't forecast wind within 1,500 feet of the station's elevation, so there's nothing at 3,000, which is underground, or at 6,000, which is only about 570 feet above it. They don't forecast temperature within 2,500 feet of the station either, and the 3,000 foot level never gets a temperature anywhere. A blank just means nobody forecast it, so don't fill it in with calm.

The prog charts are forecasts drawn as maps. The Low Level Significant Weather chart covers the surface up to FL240, at 12 and 24 hours ahead, and it comes out four times a day. It shows areas of IFR and marginal VFR, moderate or greater turbulence, and freezing levels. It doesn't show icing, which surprises people. The surface prog next to it shows the fronts and the highs and lows where they're expected to be. For planning, the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation page puts most of this on one map, and the convective outlook tells you days ahead whether thunderstorms are on the menu. One more for the list. The Ceiling and Visibility Analysis, CVA, is a map of what the ceilings and visibility are right now, built from observations and colored by flight category. It's an analysis, not a forecast. Use it to see where the low stuff is between the reporting stations, and then go read the METARs.

How the exam asks it. No wind is forecast within 1,500 feet of the station. No temperature within 2,500 feet, and none at 3,000 feet. Decode the plus 50 trick. Temperatures above 24,000 are negative without a sign.
Advisories are the warnings. Three flavors, and the test wants you to know which is which.

AIRMETs are for hazards that matter to light airplanes and VFR pilots, which is to say you, in Biscuit. Over the lower 48 they're graphical now, the G-AIRMETs, issued every 6 hours with snapshots every 3 hours out to 12 hours. If one snapshot shows nothing and the next shows a hazard, assume it started right after the first one. They come in three names. Sierra is IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango is moderate turbulence, sustained surface wind over 30 knots, and low level wind shear. Zulu is moderate icing and freezing levels. S for sky, T for turbulence, Z for, I don't know, frozen. It works for me.

A SIGMET, without the word convective in front of it, is for things that are dangerous to every airplane: severe or extreme turbulence, severe icing, widespread dust or sand storms, and volcanic ash. It's good for up to 4 hours.

A Convective SIGMET is the thunderstorm one. They come out every hour at 55 minutes past and each is good for 2 hours. One gets issued for a line of thunderstorms at least 60 miles long with storms along at least 40 percent of it, or an area of strong storms covering at least 40 percent of the area, or embedded or severe storms expected for more than 30 minutes, any size. A special one can go out for tornadoes, hail three quarters of an inch or bigger, or surface gusts of 50 knots or more. Here's the part to tattoo somewhere: a Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing, and low level wind shear, whether it says so or not.

PIREPs are pilot reports, and they're the only weather product made of actual airplanes. UA is routine, UUA is urgent. The required parts are the location after /OV, the time in Zulu after /TM, the altitude after /FL, the aircraft type after /TP, and at least one weather element, like /SK for sky, /TB for turbulence, /IC for icing. Every altitude in a PIREP is MSL, including cloud bases and tops. You give them to ATC or Flight Service. If you find something nobody warned you about, you're the warning.
How the exam asks it. Sierra, Tango, Zulu by content. Non convective SIGMET criteria. Convective SIGMET criteria and what it implies. PIREP altitudes are MSL.

A thunderstorm needs three things: enough moisture, unstable air, and something to lift it. Fronts lift air. So does heating, and so does wind blowing up a slope. Here in summer, the sun cooks the mountains and the high ground all morning, the upslope wind feeds them, and by early afternoon you'll watch towers go up over the foothills and the Palmer Divide, south of us, right on schedule. Then they drift out over the plains.

A single cell lives about 30 minutes. It starts in the cumulus stage, which the newest weather handbook calls the towering cumulus stage, and it's all updraft, sometimes more than 3,000 feet a minute. The mature stage starts when the rain reaches the ground. Now there are updrafts and downdrafts side by side, the downdraft spreads out along the surface as a gust front, and the hazards peak toward the end of this stage. The dissipating stage is mostly downdrafts. The rain tapers off and what's left is an anvil.

The hazards are the whole list. Turbulence inside and around, sometimes 20 miles out from a severe one. Hail, even under the anvil in clear air. Lightning. A gust front that can run 15 miles ahead of the rain and flip your wind around on short final. And the microburst, a column of air slamming down and spreading out, usually less than 2 and a half miles across, living 5 to 15 minutes, with downdrafts up to 6,000 feet a minute. Fly through one on approach and here's the order: first a headwind that makes the airplane feel great, then the downdraft, then a tailwind that eats your airspeed right when you need it, close to the ground. On dry Colorado afternoons the only warning might be virga, rain falling out of the base and evaporating before it lands, or a ring of dust on the ground.

Rules. Severe storm, 20 miles, minimum. Never under one, even when you can see daylight through the rain on the other side. Storm coming at the airport? Then you're not taking off and you're not landing. That weather picture on the panel GPS can be 15 or 20 minutes stale, and a cell only lives about 30, so you're looking at a storm's baby pictures. Can't get around? Land someplace and go buy a sad sandwich out of a vending machine. I've done it. The sandwich was terrible and I'm still alive.
How the exam asks it. Three ingredients. Three stages, and which one starts with rain at the surface and which one is mostly downdrafts. The microburst sequence. The 20 mile rule.
Fog, frost, icing, and mountain wave.

Fog's just cloud that sat down. You get it when temperature and dewpoint come together, or close, and you rarely get it with a spread over 2°C. So a METAR that says 09/08 should make your neck prickle. The kinds are named for how they got there. Radiation fog: clear sky, calm or nearly calm, damp air, the ground cooling all night. That one usually clears out by late morning. Advection fog: wet air blowing in over colder ground or water, which is a California problem more than ours, and it needs wind and it lingers. Upslope fog is ours. Damp, stable air gets pushed uphill by wind until it's cooled down to its dewpoint, and the handbook literally uses the eastern slope of the Rockies as the example. Hi. Because the wind's what's making it, it sticks around as long as the east wind does, sun or no sun. Steam fog is frigid air over warmer water, little wisps off a lake. Frontal fog is rain falling into cold air under a front.

Frost happens when the skin of the airplane drops below freezing and below the dewpoint of the air right against it, so the water skips being water and goes straight to ice crystals. Looks like nothing. Feels like sandpaper to the air going over your wing, which costs you lift and adds drag right when you're trying to leave the ground at 5,885 feet. Off. All of it. Every surface, tail included.

Structural ice, the kind that sticks to the airframe, takes two things: visible moisture, and the airplane being at or below freezing where the water lands. Rime is white and crusty, tiny drops that freeze the instant they touch. Clear ice comes from fat drops that smear back along the wing before they freeze, so it's glassy and heavy and hard to see, and it's the nastier of the two. If it's freezing rain where you are, the rain was liquid higher up, so there's warmer air on top of you. Ice pellets mean that freezing rain is happening above you. Biscuit's not certified for icing. You're not either. Cloud plus freezing temperatures equals somewhere else.

Last one, and it's the one that lives next door. Strong wind hitting the mountains more or less head on goes over the top and then bounces, up and down, for miles downwind, like a creek running over a rock. When there's enough moisture, the tops of those bounces make lenticulars. Smooth. Lens shaped. Parked in one spot in a gale, sometimes stacked up like a pile of plates. There might be a cap cloud hugging the ridge. And under the wave crests, down near ridge height on the downwind side, there's the rotor, a big tumbling roll of air, and the rotor's where turbulence gets severe or worse. Rotor clouds look torn and ragged, like they're being stirred. The sinking air on the lee side of a ridge can beat anything Biscuit's got for climb. Dry day? No clouds, same wave, no warning. If a METAR remark says ACSL with a direction after it, the observer saw lenticulars that way. Believe them.

How the exam asks it. Fog types by cause, with upslope fog needing wind. Frost removal. Icing needs visible moisture and freezing temperatures. Lenticulars mean mountain wave and possible rotor below.
Decision one. Sixteen gusting twenty seven.

At 5:55 the wind outside her bedroom window was pushing the neighbor's recycling bin up the sidewalk one lurch at a time. Jordan sat on the edge of the bed with her phone and pulled the weather before she'd put her feet on the floor.

Centennial, Thursday, 5:53 AM. The METAR: wind three one zero at sixteen knots, gusting twenty seven. Ten miles visibility. A few clouds at eight thousand, scattered at twelve thousand. Temperature twelve, dewpoint minus three, altimeter thirty oh two. After the remarks, A O two, then a peak wind of three one zero at thirty one knots at eleven twenty eight Zulu, and the T group, T zero one one seven one zero two eight. The TAF starts at twelve hundred Zulu with the same sixteen gusting twenty seven. From sixteen hundred Zulu, three two zero at twenty, gusting thirty two, scattered at ten thousand. From oh two hundred Zulu, three three zero at ten, sky clear.

Taped inside her kneeboard was the card Abby had written for her after the carb ice lesson, in blocky marker: STUDENT LIMITS. YOURS UNTIL I SAY. WIND 15. GUSTS NO MORE THAN 10 OVER. CROSSWIND 8. YOU MAKE THE CALL. I'LL TELL YOU IF IT'S WRONG.
It was 6:00. The lesson was at 7.
The METAR shows 16 gusting 27, and the TAF builds the wind at 1600Z. What should Jordan do?
A. Text Abby that she's canceling, with the gusts now and the stronger wind due at ten.
B. Fly it. The strong wind doesn't start until FM141600, and that's four this afternoon.
C. Drive to the airport and decide there, after she's seen the windsock with her own eyes.
D. Send Abby the METAR and TAF and ask her whether they're flying today or not.

She types it the way she'd call in a patient. Canceling. METAR 310 at 16 gust 27, peak 31 half an hour ago. TAF has 20 gust 32 from 1600Z, that's 10 local. Over the card on every line. She hits send and sits there in her socks. Ninety seconds, about. Then the phone buzzes against her knee. That's the first smart thing you've done. No emoji, no punctuation to soften it, which from Abby is practically a hug. A second bubble: Briefing room at 8 anyway. Bring coffee. Not the gas station kind.

That's it. The current report is already over every limit on the card, and the forecast says it gets worse at 1600Z, which is 10 a.m. here. Cancel early, cancel with the numbers, and I don't have to talk you out of anything. This is what the card is for.

The briefing room window buzzed in its frame whenever a gust came over the ramp, and by 8:15 it was buzzing pretty much full time. Somebody had taped a sign over the light switch that said DO NOT TOUCH THERMOSTAT (RUSS). Abby had copied the morning METAR onto the whiteboard in red marker, all of it, and drawn a fat lopsided box around the end.
Everything after RMK. People skip it. A machine stood out on that field all night measuring this stuff for you, and people skip it. She capped the marker. AO2. And the T group. Go.
How should Jordan decode the remarks in the morning METAR?
A. AO2 is an automated station with a rain sensor. The T group says 11.7 and plus 2.8.
B. AO2 means an observer added to the report. The T group is the temperature, 11.7 and 10.28.
C. AO2 is the station type, and PK WND 31031/1128 means the gusts should peak at 31 by 11:28.
D. AO2 is an automated station that can tell rain from snow. The T group reads 11.7 and minus 2.8.

AO2 is the automated station that can tell rain from snow. The T group is eleven point seven and minus two point eight. Yep. Zero's plus, one's minus, three digits each, in tenths. Up top it got rounded to 12 and M03. She writes the spread, 14.5, under the box and circles it twice, hard enough that the marker squeaks. Real spread. Remember it. One of these days some kid's going to ask you how high the clouds are and you'll get to be insufferable.

Yep. That's the one. AO2 means automated with a precipitation discriminator. AO1 has no discriminator. The T group is plus 11.7 and minus 2.8 Celsius. The body rounds to whole degrees, so the T group is what you want when the math needs precision.
Walt came in at nine with a box of grocery store donuts, set it on the table, and didn't sit down. Russ says you canceled.

Hm. He picked up a marker, uncapped it, and wrote a METAR on the board from memory in small square capitals, the way a man writes something he's written ten thousand times. Denver, January, some year. I was on shift. Where's the ceiling?

Denver, oh four fifty three Zulu on the fourteenth. Wind zero three zero at eleven, three miles in light snow and mist. Scattered at six hundred, broken at twelve hundred, overcast at three thousand. Minus one and minus two, altimeter thirty oh eight.
Walt's January METAR has scattered, broken and overcast layers. What's the ceiling?
A. 600 feet. The lowest layer reported is the ceiling, whatever the coverage says.
B. 3,000 feet. Only an overcast layer counts as a real ceiling in a METAR.
C. 1,200 feet AGL, from the broken layer.
D. 1,200 feet above sea level, the lowest broken layer in the report.

Twelve hundred. The broken layer. Walt caps the marker. Twelve hundred above the ground, three miles in snow. I dispatched into that more times than I can count, and I never once sent a Cessna. He takes a donut for himself, which Abby will tell her later is the closest thing to a compliment he has. On his way out he stops at the door. Danny would've gone this morning, you know. He'd have found a reason. He doesn't say whether that's praise or not.
Exactly right. Lowest broken or overcast layer, heights in hundreds of feet above ground level. BKN012 is a 1,200 foot AGL ceiling. The scattered layer under it doesn't count.
After Walt left, Abby turned around the whiteboard, where she'd already written the morning TAF, and underlined FM141600 twice.
Last thing before the boring part. When does this start? On a watch. Not a computer.
The coffee maker gurgled. Out on the ramp a Piper Warrior strained at its tiedowns like a dog that wanted to go for a walk.
What local time is FM141600 in Colorado in May?
A. Nine this morning, because Colorado is seven hours behind Zulu time.
B. Ten this morning. Mountain Daylight Time is six hours behind Zulu.
C. Ten tonight. You add six hours to Zulu to get to Mountain Daylight Time.
D. Four this afternoon. It reads like a clock, 16 means 1600, so four.

Ten. Six hours back in the summer. Abby checks her phone. Which is forty one minutes from now. At 10:04 the window behind her rattles in its frame hard enough that they both look at it, and the windsock across the ramp goes from straight out to straight out and angry. Abby doesn't say anything. She doesn't have to.
That's it. Subtract 6 hours in summer, on daylight time, and 7 in winter. 1600Z minus 6 is 1000 local. Every time in a METAR, TAF, AIRMET, SIGMET, PIREP, and winds aloft forecast is Zulu.
Friday night Abby sent homework instead of a time.
A text from Abby Strand. Sat 7am if it's legal and smart. We're climbing to 7,500 over Bennett. Decode the DEN line for me. Why is half of it missing?

Winds and temperatures aloft for Denver, valid twelve hundred Zulu Saturday. The three thousand and six thousand columns are blank. Nine thousand: two six one four, plus oh five. Twelve thousand: two seven two five, minus oh one. Eighteen thousand: two seven four one, minus fourteen. Twenty four thousand: two seven five two, minus twenty six. Thirty thousand: seven six zero two four one.
Jordan worked it out on the back of a pizza flyer. Then she stared at the gaps for a while, the way she'd stare at an empty line on a patient chart.
What does the DEN 9,000 foot group say, and what do the empty columns mean?
A. 9,000: 260 at 14 knots, plus 5. The lower levels are within 1,500 feet of Denver's elevation.
B. 9,000: 260 at 14, plus 5°C. Nothing at 6,000 because the winds there are light and variable.
C. 9,000: 260 at 14 knots, minus 5°C, since the temperature is always below zero up there.
D. 9,000: 140 at 26, plus 5°C. The blanks mean the data didn't come in from the station.

She texts Abby one line: the low levels are too close to the ground at Denver. Abby texts back: Yes. 3,000 is underground and 6,000 is 570 feet off the ground at DEN. No wind within 1,500 of the station, no temps within 2,500. A minute later: Bonus. Decode 30,000. Jordan subtracts 50 from 76, adds 100 to 02, and sends it: 260 at 102, minus 41. Abby: Show off. See you at 7.

Yep. That's the one. 2614+05 is 260 degrees true at 14 knots, plus 5 Celsius. Winds aren't forecast within 1,500 feet of the station's elevation and temperatures aren't forecast within 2,500 feet, and the 3,000 foot level never carries a temperature. 760241 is 260 at 102 knots, minus 41 Celsius.
Decision six. Tango over the Divide.
Twenty five minutes later the club chat lit up.

A message from Russ Kim. taking biscuit to steamboat sunday morning, it's on the calendar, don't me. yes i see the airmets. they're airmets. sigmets are the scary ones. airmets are for gliders and nervous people

Jordan opened the graphical AIRMETs on the aviation weather site. Over the mountains west of Denver on Sunday morning there was a Tango box, moderate turbulence below 18,000, and a Sierra box stuck to the high terrain for mountain obscuration. She'd known Russ for about five weeks, and most of it had been skull emojis.
Russ says AIRMETs are for gliders and nervous people. How should Jordan answer him?
A. Send Walt a private message about it and let him be the one to deal with Russ.
B. Agree with him. AIRMETs are the mild ones, and the real warnings come as SIGMETs.
C. Reply that Tango means moderate turbulence and Sierra hides the mountains, on his route.
D. Say nothing. She's a student, and Russ is the pilot in command of his own flight.

She types it plainly and adds: The Tango and the Sierra are both over your route Sunday. Not my call, you're the pilot. Just saying what they say. Nothing for four minutes. Then Russ: ok who taught the student to read. Walt: Nobody. She read it. Russ: fine. moving it to next weekend. bringing donuts as penance. marisol do not say anything. Marisol sends a single photo of the whiteboard: ELT BATT, boxed.

Exactly right. Sierra is IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango is moderate turbulence, strong surface wind, and low level wind shear. Zulu is icing and freezing levels. Those are aimed at light airplanes. Saying the facts without the attitude is how a student talks to a pilot with a thousand hours.
Decision seven. Sugar on the wing.

Saturday came up clear and dead calm. ATIS: minus one, dewpoint minus three. Biscuit had spent the night tied down on the ramp like always, and in the blue light before sunrise her wings had gone fuzzy. Powdered sugar. On May 16th. Colorado.
Jordan dragged a fingertip down the leading edge and it left a clean wet stripe of maroon paint. You could read the N number on the tail right through the stuff. Abby's text said ten minutes out.
The wings are frosted at sunrise after a night tied down at minus one. What should Jordan do?
A. Polish it smooth with a soft towel, so it's flat and won't disturb the air.
B. Push Biscuit out into the sun and wait until every bit of frost is gone.
C. Clear the wings, and leave the thin frost on the tail. It's a small surface.
D. Go. It's so thin it'll blow off in the first few seconds of the takeoff roll.

They tow her to the east end of the row, where the sun clears the hangars first, and stand around in it like cows. Forty minutes. Marisol wanders over in a parka with three coffees in a cardboard tray and one of them has JORDAN written on the lid. Danny used to come out with a squeegee and a thermos of hot water. Then he'd stand there yelling at the water for freezing on the windshield. She hands it over. Sun's better. Sun doesn't need a thermos. Wheels up at 7:42, bare dry wings.

That's it. The PHAK says an aircraft must be thoroughly cleaned and free of frost before flight. Sun, a heated hangar, or approved deicing all work. Waiting costs a lesson slot. Frost on takeoff can cost the airplane.
Decision eight. Flat on the bottom.

Sunday was a cookout at Claire's in Parker. Burgers, on the enormous grill Danny bought the summer he decided he was a grill guy and then used maybe nine times. The patio umbrella was still in its winter cover. His orange Broncos camp chair was still folded up against the back fence with a dried leaf stuck in the hinge. It had been there since March.

Ellie was flat on her back on the trampoline in shin guards and one sock, eating a pickle. Ellie's other sock was on the grass, nowhere near the trampoline. Above her the clouds were coming off the foothills in a herd, big lumpy white ones, and every last one had a bottom so flat you could've set a level on it. Same height, every one. Like a glass shelf.
Aunt Jordan. Why are clouds flat on the bottom?
Somewhere down the block a dog kept barking at nothing. Claire looked over from the grill with the spatula in her hand. She didn't say anything. Danny had been the one for questions like this.
Which answer is the real reason cumulus bases line up?
A. The wind blows along under them all day, and it flattens the bottoms out.
B. Warm air rises and cools, and the cloud starts at the height where it cools to its dewpoint.
C. Clouds float on a layer of heavier air under them, kind of like ice on water.
D. It gets colder the higher you go, and the clouds start where it's cold enough up there.

Getting onto a trampoline at thirty five turns out to involve a knee and some swearing under her breath. She lies down next to Ellie anyway. Okay. Driveway gets hot, right? Burns your feet. It heats up the air sitting on it, and hot air goes up. Bubble in a pot of water. But up is colder, so the bubble cools off on the way. And there's water hiding in it. Invisible. Cool it enough and, boom, you can see it. Like your breath in January. Jordan laughs. Like your breath in January. And all the bubbles around here started out about the same, so they all hit cold enough at the same height. That's your shelf. Ellie squints up at it for a while. So the shelf is made of cold. Kind of. You can figure out how high it is with a thermometer. Ellie sits up. Show me. Over at the grill Claire flips a burger she's already flipped, and her shoulders drop about an inch.

Yep. That's the one. Rising air cools at about 3 degrees Celsius per 1,000 feet and its dewpoint drops about half a degree, so they meet at a predictable height. Air with the same surface temperature and dewpoint condenses at the same level, which is why the bases line up flat.

May 28th, a Thursday, and Centennial was showing off. Calm, cool, the windsock hanging like a sleeve. Out west over Evergreen, though, three long gray clouds sat stacked one on another like plates in a cupboard, not moving, edges so smooth they looked cut out with scissors. A guy fueling a Mooney had his phone up taking pictures.

Centennial, Thursday, 6:53 AM. Wind two three zero at four, ten miles, a few clouds at fifteen thousand, nine and minus one, altimeter twenty nine eighty eight. And in the remarks, standing lenticular altocumulus, west through northwest.

The winds aloft over the Divide were 270 at 45 at 12,000. Jordan had looked them up because now she couldn't help it. It was 48 degrees and she was in a fleece she'd regret by ten. Abby was doing the walkaround. Those are pretty. Where do you want to go?
A. Cancel the whole lesson. Lenticulars mean the air everywhere is too rough today.
B. Climb high toward them and ride the lift, the way glider pilots do on wave days.
C. Stay east in the practice area as planned, and keep well away from the foothills.
D. Fly west toward them, but stay well underneath, so they can get a good look safely.

East. The practice area, nowhere near the foothills. Good. Lenticulars. Forty five knots coming over the Divide, and it's sloshing on the far side like a bathtub, and under the sloshing there's rotor. Gorgeous. From Bennett. An hour of smooth air over the wheat. Jordan keeps twisting around in her seat to look at them, which costs her fifty feet on a steep turn and an eyebrow from Abby.

Exactly right. Altocumulus standing lenticular clouds are the classic sign of mountain wave. The METAR even flagged them in the remarks, west through northwest. The turbulence and rotor are on the lee side near the mountains, so the smart plan stays east and keeps distance from the foothills.

The first week of June turned hot. Abby moved the lessons earlier, and still, by 10 a.m. the air over the plains east of the airport was boiling up off the wheat fields. At 7,500 over Bennett, Biscuit hit a bump that lifted Jordan off the seat against her belt, and then another one, and the coffee cup in the side pocket jumped out and rolled under the rudder pedals.
It went on like that for a couple of minutes. Not dangerous. Not fun either. The airspeed needle wandering ten knots each way. Abby's pen bouncing on her kneeboard.
Nobody's reported this. We're on with Denver Approach. Give them a PIREP.
What does Denver Approach need to hear about the bumps near Bennett?
A. Skip it. It's only a trainer, and big airplanes aren't going to care what a 172 feels.
B. Tell Approach it's pretty bumpy out by Bennett, so other pilots know to watch for it.
C. Report moderate turbulence near Bennett at 1,600 feet, Cessna 172, a couple of minutes ago.
D. Moderate turbulence over Bennett at 7,500, Cessna 172, with the current time.

She keys the mic and it comes out almost the way Abby taught her. Denver Approach, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, PIREP. Over Bennett, seven thousand five hundred, Cessna One Seventy Two, moderate turbulence, last two minutes. The controller reads it back and thanks her. Thirty seconds later he passes it to a Bonanza inbound from the east. Abby writes PIREP on her kneeboard and draws a star next to it.

That's it. Location, time, altitude MSL, aircraft type, and the hazard with an intensity. That's the required core of a PIREP, plus at least one weather element. Moderate means real changes in altitude or attitude with the airplane under control at all times.

A cold front came down the plains on a Friday night in June, and by Saturday morning the whole city had a lid on it. Jordan woke at 5 to a world the color of dishwater. Her own street ended in gray after about four houses.

Centennial, Saturday, 5:53 AM. The METAR: wind zero seven zero at nine, two miles in mist, overcast at four hundred feet. Temperature nine, dewpoint eight, altimeter thirty twenty one. The TAF has zero seven zero at ten, two miles in mist, overcast at four hundred, and temporarily until fifteen hundred Zulu, half a mile in fog with the overcast down to two hundred. From two thousand Zulu, zero five zero at eight, five miles in mist, broken at twelve hundred. From oh one hundred Zulu, three three zero at six, more than six miles, scattered at five thousand.
The lesson was at nine. Abby hadn't texted. Jordan understood by now that this was on purpose.
The METAR shows a one degree spread and a 400 foot overcast after a front. What should Jordan decide?
A. Go above it. The fog is only a few hundred feet thick, and it's clear on top.
B. Wait an hour or two. Morning fog always burns off once the sun gets going.
C. Fly under it. The ceiling is 400 feet, and she can stay in the pattern.
D. Cancel. It's upslope fog, and it'll stick around until the east wind stops.

She texts Abby: Canceling. East at 9, spread 1, upslope. TAF keeps it upslope all day, northeast at 2000Z, and doesn't turn it northwest till 0100Z, 7 PM. Abby: Agree. Go back to bed. Then: You're getting annoying to teach. Then: Compliment. Jordan gets back under the covers and doesn't sleep. Outside a garbage truck works its way down the block, invisible, beeping.

Yep. That's the one. East wind, a tiny spread, a low overcast after a front: textbook upslope fog. It forms when moist, stable air is pushed up rising terrain and it needs the wind to keep going. It won't burn off like radiation fog while that wind blows.
Saturday the 13th of June was the first true summer day. The TAF had a line Jordan read three times before she left the house.

The Centennial forecast, Saturday, 5:20 AM. Light and variable this morning, a few clouds at twelve thousand. From seventeen hundred Zulu, east at eight, scattered at eight thousand. From two thousand Zulu, one three zero at twelve gusting twenty, scattered at seven thousand, broken at twelve thousand. A thirty percent chance, twenty one hundred to midnight Zulu, of thunderstorms and rain, with cumulonimbus in a broken layer at six thousand. From oh two hundred Zulu, one eight zero at six, scattered at twelve thousand.

Wheels up 10:30. By ten after twelve they were doing power off stalls over the practice area, and each time she rolled out of a clearing turn the stuff to the south had grown. One cloud over the Palmer Divide, twenty five miles off, maybe, had quit being a cloud. It was a tower now. Cauliflower on top, white as a fridge, still going up, and a gray smear hanging under one side of it with ragged strings falling out of the bottom and quitting halfway to the ground.
On an ambulance she'd have called it a scene she didn't like the look of. She knew that feeling. She'd never had it at 7,500 feet.
Abby, who'd seen it ten minutes ago, said nothing at all.
A cell over the Palmer Divide is towering, with rain falling out of its base. What's Jordan's best move?
A. End the lesson now and head straight back to Centennial, before the storm gets going.
B. Fly a few miles south toward it, so she can see what a rain shaft looks like up close.
C. Keep flying. The TAF says storms after 2100Z, and that's only a 30 percent chance.
D. Finish the last stall series, ten more minutes, and then head back to Centennial.

I want to go home. Your airplane. Jordan turns west for home and calls the tower twelve miles out. The ATIS wind is still calm, if you can believe it. They land at 12:41 on 35R. After landing flow, the way Abby taught it: flaps up, carb heat cold, strobes off, mixture leaned for taxi. By 12:55 Biscuit's tied down, gust locks in. At 1:20, from the briefing room window, they watch a wall of brown dust come up the airport from the south and the windsock snap around to point north, and every tied down airplane on the ramp rocks on its ropes at once. Abby checks her watch, then the TAF on her phone. Forty minutes early, she says. Write that down somewhere.

Exactly right. Towering cumulus with virga and a rain shaft means a cell in or near the mature stage. The gust front can arrive well ahead of the rain, and the TAF's timing is a guess. Heading home early, while the home airport is still calm, is the whole plan.

Jordan drove to Parker with the windows down, which was a mistake for about three minutes when the outflow caught her on Parker Road and threw grit across the windshield, and then the air went cool and smelled like wet pavement, and it was the best thing she'd smelled all week.

Claire's kitchen window faced south, over the back fence and the camp chair and the neighbors' roofs, all the way to the long dark rise of the Palmer Divide. The storm was sitting right on top of it. The anvil had spread out across half the sky, flat and white, and under it the base was the color of a bruise, with rain hanging down in sheets you could see move.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Mija the news says hail in Castle Rock. Tell me you are not in that airplane.

She texts back: On the ground since 12:41. At Claire's. Watching it from the kitchen. A pause, the three dots coming and going for a long time. Then: Good. Kiss Ellie. Which was, from her mother, about a paragraph.

Ellie knelt on a kitchen chair with her nose almost on the glass, counting between the flashes and the thunder. Claire stood behind her with a dish towel over her shoulder. Jordan had the green notebook on the counter. She'd brought it on purpose. She'd read ahead last night, finally, and found the page she wanted.

Danny's logbook, a page from June, six years ago. June 17. KAPA to KCOS for lunch, return via KFLY, 2.1. TAF said thunderstorms from 2100. Figured that's nine PM, I'll be home by four, easy. Reader, 2100 Zulu is THREE PM. Found this out at 3 PM over Monument with a black wall in front of me and a Bonanza on frequency asking ATC if anybody knew where the gust front was. Landed Meadow Lake. Ate vending machine peanut butter crackers in the FBO for two hours and watched it rain on my plans. Zulu is not a suggestion. Zulu is six hours from my watch. In the winter it's seven, which I will also forget.

Jordan read it out loud. Claire laughed before she got to the crackers, and then put the dish towel over her face for a second, and when she took it down she said, He called me from the vending machine. I remember. He said he was being responsible and he wanted credit for it. She looked over at Jordan. Abby texted me. I didn't know Abby had my number. It just said, she turned around early and didn't argue. That's the whole text.
Is Daddy's writing in there about clouds? Ellie said, without turning around from the window.
About a storm. He got stuck somewhere and had to wait it out.
Jordan looked down at the page. The handwriting got bigger in the part about the black wall. Some. Then he landed and ate crackers out of a machine for two hours. Which was the smart part.

Ellie chewed on that. Out over the Divide the rain was dragging itself back south, the dark flat base lifting off the hilltops like a lid coming off a pot, and way behind it there was a strip of that hard rinsed blue you only get afterward. Is the flat part the shelf?
Same shelf, Jordan said. Somebody just piled way too much on it.
Claire's hand went to the back of Ellie's chair. Then, after a second, to Jordan's shoulder, and it stayed there while the thunder grumbled off toward Kansas and the gutters ran.
